title: How to Make a Geometry Dash-Style Rhythm Platformer on iPad
summary: Build a Geometry Dash-style rhythm platformer on iPad with hyperPad: a tap-to-jump loop, obstacles timed to the beat, fast restarts and clear feedback.
body_markdown:
You can make a Geometry Dash-style rhythm platformer on iPad with hyperPad. Start with one tap-to-jump loop, a few obstacles timed to the beat, and fast restarts. This guide shows you how to build that loop with physics, Attributes and visual Behaviors, then grow it into a full level.


*Geometry Dash is made by RobTop Games, and hyperPad has no affiliation with it. Use the game as a design reference only. Build original art, audio, levels and branding for your own Project.*


The screenshots in this guide come from[The Wave](https://www.hyperpad.com/projects/9tfx3yz6) by RobinsonX, a one-touch game made in hyperPad and published on the hyperPad Hub. Play it to see these ideas in a finished game.


## What makes a rhythm platformer work


A good rhythm platformer makes one input feel important. The player reads an obstacle, commits to a jump, hears the beat, and sees the result right away.


RobTop describes Geometry Dash as a rhythm-based action platformer with one-touch play. That points to four design questions for your own game:


1. Can the player understand the input immediately?
2. Can they read the next obstacle before reaching it?
3. Does the audio support the level's timing?
4. Does failure show them what to try next?


Your goal is a clear relationship between input, movement, obstacle spacing, sound and feedback. You learn that by building and testing your own level.


## Build one jump loop


Start with one Scene and five Objects:


- a dynamic player Object
- a ground Object
- one obstacle
- a tap area: a large Object that covers the screen, with its opacity set to 0
- a restart button


Add a number Attribute named` canJump` to the player. Use` 1` when the player is on the ground and` 0` while airborne.


[Started Touching](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/started-touching) fires when its Object A is touched. Set Object A to the tap area, so a tap anywhere on the screen counts. Then build this Behavior chain:


1. **Started Touching** fires when the player taps the screen.
2. An[If](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/if) checks whether` canJump` equals` 1` .
3. [Set Attribute](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/set-attribute) changes` canJump` to` 0` .
4. [Set Velocity](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/set-velocity) gives the player upward movement.
5. [Play Sound](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/play-sound) plays a short jump cue.


Together, these Behaviors make a small flowchart of your game's logic. A tap starts it, the If checks the player's state, and the actions change that state and move the player with physics.


## Restore the jump after landing


Add a[Collision Event](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/collision-event) and use its **Started Colliding** event. Set Object A to the player and Object B to the ground, and turn on **On Top** . Connect it to a Set Attribute that changes` canJump` back to` 1` .


On Top means the jump only comes back when the player lands on the ground. Brushing the side of an obstacle won't give the player a free jump.


*The whole jump loop at a glance. Build the top chain first, then the landing chain under it.*


Test this before adding more obstacles:


- tapping on the ground produces one jump
- tapping repeatedly in the air doesn't create extra jumps
- landing restores the next jump
- the player doesn't snag on the obstacle or the ground edge


If the controls feel unclear, fix this loop first. A longer level will magnify a weak jump.


## Design obstacle rhythm


Obstacle spacing decides when the player must act. Treat each gap as a timing decision.


*In The Wave, every corner of the path is a timing decision, and the player can read the next turn well before reaching it.*


Begin with three obstacles:


- one comfortable jump
- one jump that needs a later tap
- one pair that tests recovery after landing


Run the Scene and note where you tap. If an obstacle surprises you before you can read it, move it farther away or simplify the art around it. If every jump has the same timing, change the spacing.


A[Timer](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/timer) can drive repeating systems, but use it with care. The documentation warns that too many timers firing at 0 seconds can slow your game down.


## Connect sound to gameplay


A level feels rhythmic when the player's actions and the level's visual events line up with what they hear. Place obstacles so the jumps land on beats you can count.


Use short sounds for actions that need instant confirmation:


- jump
- landing
- collectible pickup
- checkpoint
- failure


Use Play Sound for those short effects. For the soundtrack, use[Play Music](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/play-music) instead, so you can balance the music and the effects separately. For an original level, use audio you made or have permission to use.


## Make failure useful


When the player hits an obstacle, connect a Collision Event for the player and the obstacle to a short response:


1. stop player input
2. play a failure sound
3. trigger[Shake Screen](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/shake-screen) with small values
4. show the restart button
5. reset the Scene when the player taps restart


*A clear failure moment in The Wave: the trail breaks apart where the player left the path, so it's obvious what went wrong.*


The player should know what happened and how to try again without hunting through the screen. Fast restarts are a big part of why the genre feels fair.


## Add visual feedback with purpose


Add polish after the controls and timing work. Useful options in hyperPad include:


- animation for takeoff and landing
- particles for a collectible or checkpoint
- a small camera or screen response on failure
- a Label that shows attempts or progress
- a color change when the player reaches a new section


*The Wave changes its whole color scheme between sections. The floating particles add movement, but they stay faint so the path is still easy to read.*


Test each effect while the game is moving. Remove anything that hides the next obstacle or makes the input harder to read.


## A practical test checklist


Play the level ten times and note the result of each run.


- Did every touch produce the expected action?
- Could you see each obstacle early enough to decide?
- Did the landing state reset every time?
- Did the sound confirm actions without drowning out the music?
- Was it clear why you failed?
- Could you restart immediately?
- Did visual effects keep the obstacles readable?


Change one thing at a time. Adjust jump velocity, obstacle spacing or feedback separately so you can tell which change helped.


## Grow the Project after the first loop works


Once the three-obstacle test feels consistent, expand the Project with:


- a second Scene with a different timing pattern
- collectibles that reward a harder route
- an attempt counter stored in an Attribute
- checkpoints for a longer level
- a menu and a level-select screen
- original animation, music and environment art


When it's ready for feedback, Publish the Project to the hyperPad Hub and ask players which jump felt unfair. hyperPad Starter can Publish one Project to the Hub. To put your game on the App Store, use hyperPad, the paid app: you Export from hyperPad, then sign and submit with Xcode on a Mac and an Apple Developer account.
